corpus_definition: a belief or activity passed down through many years.

forms.definition: a custom or belief passed from parents to children over many years
forms.example: It is a family tradition to eat plov together on Fridays.

syn.note: Very close; a custom is often what people in one place usually do.
More formal: a usual way of doing things that most people accept.
Related: something people do regularly, but it does not have to be old.
Related: all the history, culture and customs that a group has.

forms.note: There is no verb made from tradition.

forms.definition: following customs and beliefs that have existed for a long time
forms.example: The women wore traditional dresses at the wedding in Bukhara.

syn.note: Formal: what people usually do in a place or situation.
Close, but often about style or ideas that are normal, not exciting.
Related: a classic style is old but still popular and good.
Related, but negative: no longer modern or popular.

ant.note: Modern things are new and do not follow old customs.

forms.definition: according to customs that have existed for a long time
forms.example: Traditionally, the bride's family prepares the food for the guests.

syn.note: Formal and less common.
In the normal, accepted way.
Related and easy: what happens most of the time, not always because of old customs.

people.definition: a person who likes old customs and does not like change
people.example: My grandfather is a traditionalist and does not like modern music.

context.text: In Uzbekistan, it is a tradition to give guests tea first. My grandmother still cooks traditional food for Navruz. Traditionally, the whole family helps her in the kitchen.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged into one map; no verb exists in this family.

corpus_definition: a very sad event that causes great suffering or loss

forms.definition: a very sad event that causes great suffering, death or loss
forms.example: The plane crash was a terrible tragedy for the families.

syn.note: Close; a disaster is often bigger, like a flood or an earthquake.
A very big disaster; more formal.
Related: bad luck; usually much smaller than a tragedy.

forms.note: There is no verb made from tragedy.

forms.definition: very sad, often because someone has died or suffered
forms.example: Her uncle died in a tragic accident last year.

syn.note: Close: so sad that it makes you feel great pain inside.
Close: causing great damage or very strong sadness.
Related and easy, but weaker: tragic means very sad and serious.
Related: very bad, but not always about death or loss.

forms.definition: in a very sad way, often when someone dies young
forms.example: Tragically, the young driver died in the crash.

syn.note: Easy and softer; used for many kinds of bad news.
Related: used for bad news that is not always very serious.

context.text: The earthquake was a tragedy for the whole town. Many families lost their homes, and tragically, some people died. Everyone talked about the tragic news for weeks.

reviewer_note: Only the 'sad event' sense; tragedian (actor or writer of tragic plays) is rare and belongs to the theatre sense, so it is left out. No affix claimed: trag- is not a word.

corpus_definition: The result of changing text into a different language.

forms.definition: a text or speech changed into a different language
forms.example: The translation was quite difficult to read.

syn.note: Related: one form of a text, for example the Uzbek version of a book.
Related: usually spoken, done while someone is talking.

forms.definition: to change words from one language into another
forms.example: Can you translate this letter into Russian for me?

syn.note: Interpret is for spoken words; translate is usually for written text.
Related: to change something into a different form, not only language.

forms.definition: possible to put into another language
forms.example: Some jokes are not easily translatable.

ant.note: Impossible to put into another language and keep the same meaning.

forms.note: There is no common adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person whose job is changing texts between languages
people.example: She works as a professional translator.

context.text: My sister wants to translate Uzbek poems into English. She says a good translation needs a lot of time. One day she hopes to work as a translator.

reviewer_note: interpreter is a near-synonym person noun but not made from translate, so it is in people_not_family.

corpus_definition: A person whose job is to change text between languages.

forms.definition: a person whose job is changing texts between languages
forms.example: She works as a professional translator.

syn.note: An interpreter changes spoken words; a translator usually works with written text.

forms.definition: a text changed into a different language
forms.example: The English translation of the book came out last year.

syn.note: Related: one form of a text, for example the Russian version.

forms.definition: to change words from one language into another
forms.example: He translates books from Russian into Uzbek.

syn.note: Interpret is for spoken words; translate is usually for written text.

forms.definition: possible to put into another language
forms.example: Poems are often hardly translatable.

ant.note: Impossible to put into another language and keep the same meaning.

forms.note: There is no common adverb in this family.

context.text: My cousin is a translator in Tashkent. She can translate documents from English, Russian and Turkish. Her last translation was a long business contract.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6); translation is an extra noun entry.

corpus_definition: Ways to move people or goods from place to place.

forms.definition: ways of moving people or goods from one place to another
forms.example: We need better public transportation in this city.
forms.note: Mostly American English; British English usually says transport.

syn.note: American English, mostly for buses and trains in a city: public transit.
Related: the act of going from place to place.
Related: moving goods, often by sea or by truck.

forms.definition: the system of buses, trains and cars for travelling
forms.example: Public transport in Tashkent is cheap and fast.

forms.definition: to take people or goods from one place to another
forms.example: Trucks transport cotton from the fields to the factory.

syn.note: Easy and general; carry is also used for a person holding something.
Easy and very general.
Related: to send goods, often by sea, plane or truck.
Related: to bring something to the person who should get it.

forms.definition: easy to move from one place to another
forms.example: This small transportable heater is useful in winter.

syn.note: More common; small and light enough to carry.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a large vehicle that carries cars or other heavy things
people.example: A car transporter blocked the road this morning.

context.text: Public transportation in Tashkent is cheap and fast. The metro can transport thousands of people every hour, so many students use it every day.

reviewer_note: transport is both a noun (British) and a verb; the noun is an extra existing entry. portable is not a family member, only a synonym.

corpus_definition: Things done by doctors to cure a sickness.

forms.definition: medical care that doctors give to cure an illness or injury
forms.example: The patient needs urgent medical treatment today.

syn.note: Close; therapy is often a longer kind of help, like physical therapy.
Related: general help for sick people, as in medical care.
Related: something that cures a problem, often a home remedy.
Related: a cure makes the illness go away; a treatment may not.

forms.definition: to give medical care to a sick or hurt person
forms.example: The doctor treated him for a bad cough.

syn.note: Related: cure means the illness is gone; treat means you try to help.
Related: to make a wound or sick person healthy again.
Related and easy: to look after someone who is ill.
Related: to look after a sick person until they are better.

ant.note: To not give someone the care they need.

forms.definition: able to be cured or helped with medical care
forms.example: Most skin problems are treatable if you see a doctor early.

syn.note: Close, but curable means the illness can go away completely.

ant.note: It can never go away completely.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My uncle went to a clinic in Tashkent for treatment. The doctors treated his back pain with exercise and medicine. They said the problem was treatable.

reviewer_note: Two rows (B2 and B1) mean medical care, so they are merged with cefr B1. The other meaning of treatment (the way you behave towards someone) is not mapped.

corpus_definition: to cut a small amount from something to make it neat

forms.definition: a short cut that makes hair or a plant neater
forms.example: My hair needs a trim before the wedding.

syn.note: Easy and general: a cut can be short or long.
Related: only for hair, and often a bigger change.

forms.definition: decoration added along the edge of clothes or furniture
forms.example: The coat had a fur trimming around the collar.
forms.note: Belongs to trim = decorate an edge, not cutting hair or plants.

forms.definition: to cut a small amount off something to make it neat
forms.example: He asked the barber to trim his beard a little.

syn.note: Cut is general; trim means cutting only a little to make something neat.
Close: to cut with scissors, often small things like nails or hair.
Related: to make something shorter in any way.
Related: only for trees and plants.

forms.definition: cut neatly so that it is short and tidy
forms.example: He has a neatly trimmed moustache.

syn.note: Close: cut short with scissors.
Related and easy: tidy and in good order.
Related and easy: in good order.

ant.note: Grown too long and untidy, like a garden that nobody cares for.

forms.definition: thin, fit and healthy-looking
forms.example: My uncle stays trim by walking every evening.
forms.note: Belongs to trim = slim and fit, not the cutting meaning.
trimly exists but is very rare.

people.definition: a small electric tool for cutting hair, a beard or grass
people.example: Dad uses an electric trimmer for his beard.

context.text: Before Eid, my brother went to the barber for a trim. The barber trimmed his beard, and now it looks short and tidy. He loves his neatly trimmed look.

reviewer_note: trim is also an adjective meaning slim and fit (other_meaning); trimming as decoration is other_meaning too.

corpus_definition: Information that is correct and not based on lies.

forms.definition: the real facts about something, not lies
forms.example: She told the truth about what happened yesterday.

syn.note: Related: a fact is one correct piece of information; the truth is the whole real story.
Related: what really exists or happens.
Related: the quality of a person who does not lie.

ant.note: Something you say that you know is not correct.
Formal word for a statement that is not correct.

forms.note: There is no verb made from truth.

forms.definition: correct and based on facts, not invented
forms.example: Is it true that you are moving to Samarkand?

syn.note: Close; often used for answers and information.
Easy and common: 'That's right.'
Correct in every detail; a little formal.
Related: existing, not imagined: a real story.

ant.note: Same as false, a little softer.

forms.definition: always saying what really happened; honest
forms.example: He gave a truthful answer to the police.

syn.note: Very close and more common.

ant.note: Saying things that are not correct.

forms.definition: really and sincerely, in a way that is not false
forms.example: I am truly sorry for being late.

syn.note: Easy and very common.
Close: in a real way, not pretending.
Related: used for feelings, as in 'Yours sincerely'.

forms.definition: in an honest way, saying what really happened
forms.example: Please answer all the questions truthfully.

syn.note: Very close and more common.

context.text: My little brother broke the window, but he told the truth. Mum was happy that he was truthful. She said, 'It is true that everyone makes mistakes.'

reviewer_note: truth is made from true; truly is spelled without the e of true. No affix claimed on truly.

corpus_definition: the usual or normal way that someone or something acts.

forms.definition: a group of people or things that share the same features
forms.example: What type of music do you like?

syn.note: Same meaning, very easy.
Same meaning; very common in spoken British English.
Related and more formal: a group in a system.

forms.definition: to be a very good example of something
forms.example: This old house typifies the buildings of Khiva.

syn.note: Formal: to be a usual feature of something.
Formal: to be a good example of something.
Related: to stand for a group or an idea.

forms.definition: having the usual features you expect from something
forms.example: This is a typical day for me.

syn.note: Easy: what happens most often.
Easy: what people expect; not strange.
Formal: showing the special features of a person or thing.
Related: the normal or most common kind.
Related: a very good, clear example: a classic mistake.

ant.note: Not like the usual examples of something.
Formal word with the same meaning as untypical.

forms.definition: usually; in the way that happens most often
forms.example: Typically, I get home from university at six.

syn.note: Easy and very common.
Easy and very common.
Related: in most cases.

ant.note: In a way that is different from normal.

context.text: A typical morning in our house starts with green tea and bread. Typically, my father reads the news while we eat. What type of breakfast do you have?

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same 'usual' meaning merged. Verb type (use a keyboard) belongs to another meaning of type and is left out; typicality is rare.

corpus_definition: Feeling a little bit of pain or not being relaxed.

forms.definition: a feeling of slight pain or of not being relaxed
forms.example: She felt some discomfort in her back after the long bus ride.

syn.note: Related but stronger: discomfort is a small pain.
Related: a worried or nervous feeling, not about the body.
Related: a pain that continues, like a headache.

ant.note: The good feeling of being relaxed with no pain.

forms.note: There is no verb for this meaning. The verb comfort means to make someone feel less sad.

forms.definition: not relaxed, or feeling a little pain in the body
forms.example: The wooden seat was very uncomfortable.

syn.note: For feelings: worried or nervous; not used for chairs or clothes.
Related: not relaxed with other people, often embarrassed.
Related but much stronger: it really hurts.

ant.note: Relaxed, or pleasant to sit in or wear.

forms.definition: in a way that is not relaxed or pleasant
forms.example: The room was uncomfortably hot in July.

syn.note: For feelings: in a worried or nervous way.
Related: in an embarrassed or not relaxed way.

ant.note: In a relaxed and pleasant way.

context.text: The bus seats were uncomfortable, so the trip to Fergana felt very long. After six hours, I felt real discomfort in my back. I sat uncomfortably until we arrived.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a negative form; the positive family words (comfort, comfortable, comfortably) are listed as antonyms, not forms.
